title: PMFs and CDFs
short: A pmf lists P(X = x); the CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) climbs in steps, and P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).
trouble: Students use F(b) − F(a) for P(a ≤ X ≤ b) with a discrete X, which leaves out P(X = a).

blocks.html: A discrete random variable takes values you can list, each with a probability. Two descriptions carry the same information: the probability mass function lists $P(X = x)$, and the cumulative distribution function adds them up. Moving between them, with care at the endpoints, is the skill here.

The pmf is $p_X(x) = P(X = x)$: never negative, adding to 1 over all values. The CDF is $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$: it climbs in steps from 0 to 1, jumping by $P(X = a)$ at each value $a$. For $a < b$: $$P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a).$$

The events $\{X \le a\}$ and $\{a < X \le b\}$ are disjoint, and together they make $\{X \le b\}$. By the addition axiom, $F(b) = F(a) + P(a < X \le b)$. The size of a jump is a special case: $P(X = a) = F(a) - P(X < a)$, the CDF at $a$ minus its value just before $a$. Between two values of $X$ nothing happens, so $F$ is flat there: if $X$ is a whole number, $F(2.5) = F(2)$.

blocks.name: prob-density
blocks.cap: The number of heads in three fair coin flips: bars for the pmf and the step-shaped CDF below. Switch which ends count and watch the bars and the gap change.

blocks.html: On the CDF a filled dot sits at the top of each jump and an open dot at the bottom: at $x = a$ the CDF already includes $P(X = a)$.

blocks.title: Reading the CDF from the pmf
blocks.q: $X$ is the number of heads in three fair flips: $p(0) = \frac{1}{8}$, $p(1) = \frac{3}{8}$, $p(2) = \frac{3}{8}$, $p(3) = \frac{1}{8}$. Find $F(1)$, $F(1.5)$ and $P(1 \le X \le 2)$.
steps: $F(1) = p(0) + p(1) = \frac{1}{2}$, and $F(1.5) = \frac{1}{2}$ too: no value lies between 1 and 1.5.
With the CDF: $F(2) - F(0) = \frac{7}{8} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3}{4}$. Subtract $F(0)$, not $F(1)$, so that $X = 1$ stays in.

blocks.html: Using $F(b) - F(a)$ for $P(a \le X \le b)$ when $X$ is discrete. That difference is $P(a < X \le b)$ and leaves out $P(X = a)$, which can be large. Check by listing the values that should count and adding their probabilities directly. (For continuous variables single points have probability 0, so there the endpoints do not matter.)
